To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) academic motivation and social motivation variables are related to cheating; (2) social motivation variables are better predictors of cheating than academic motivation variables; (3) academic self efficacy and participation structures are better predictors of students' cheating than extrinsic and intrinsic goal orientations; and (4) the addition of social motivation variables to the academic motivation variables improves the classification rates of cheaters and noncheaters

(a) the more students feel they belong to a school, the less they cheat, (b) students who feel that their teachers are committed to them and respect them cheat less, (c) the more students believe they can succeed academically, the less they will cheat, and (d) students who are extrinsically oriented cheat more than students with an intrinsic goal orientation.

(a) academic and social motivations are both associated with cheating; (b) social motivations, such as participation in school, are more important than academic motivations in predicting cheating; and (c) the social context of the school, as measured by teacher commitment, teacher respect, teacher competence, and participation structure, is a better predictor of cheating than academic motivation.
